#### 1. glycine N-methyltransferase deficiency  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.450)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-2408508)

**Proposed mechanism:** AHCY (HGNC:254) —DISRUPTS→ S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:16783); S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:16783) —DECREASES→ Methylation (GO:0006342); Methylation (GO:0006342) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); Methylation (GO:0006342) —LEADS_TO→ Seizures (HP:0001250); Methylation (GO:0006342) —LEADS_TO→ Hypotonia (HP:0001252); GNMT (HGNC:4378) —DISRUPTS→ S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:17794); S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:17794) —DECREASES→ Methylation (GO:0006342); Methylation (GO:0006342) —LEADS_TO→ Developmental delay (HP:0001263). Mutations in AHCY lead to accumulation of S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), which inhibits numerous SAM-dependent methyltransferases, thereby decreasing global methylation. Similarly, mutations in GNMT lead to reduced conversion of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), and GNMT deficiency can paradoxically lead to altered SAM/SAH ratios and impaired methylation. Both disruptions converge on impaired cellular methylation processes, leading to shared neurological phenotypes.

**How to falsify it:** If genetic analysis reveals that the causal variants for Disease A (AHCY deficiency) and Disease B (GNMT deficiency) do not result in a significant decrease in global methylation potential or do not converge on the shared methylation pathway, this hypothesis would be falsified.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared impact on methylation could lead to therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or supplementing methylation capacity, potentially benefiting patients with either condition.

#### 2. intellectual disability, autosomal recessive 51  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.443)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-2408508)

**Proposed mechanism:** AHCY (HGNC:271) —DISRUPTS→ S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:17486); S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:17486) —LEADS_TO→ Methionine metabolism and SAM cycle (REACT:REACT-72193); Methionine metabolism and SAM cycle (REACT:REACT-72193) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); Methionine metabolism and SAM cycle (REACT:REACT-72193) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormal facial shape (HP:0001999); HNMT (HGNC:4863) —DISRUPTS→ S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:17485); S-adenosylmethionine (CHEBI:17485) —LEADS_TO→ Methionine metabolism and SAM cycle (REACT:REACT-72193); S-adenosylhomocysteine (CHEBI:17486) —INCREASES→ Homocysteine (CHEBI:17842); Homocysteine (CHEBI:17842) —LEADS_TO→ Methionine metabolism and SAM cycle (REACT:REACT-72193). Loss-of-function mutations in AHCY disrupt the hydrolysis of S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), leading to its accumulation. SAH accumulation impairs the methionine adenosyltransferase (MAT) complex, disrupting the S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) cycle and methionine metabolism. This disruption affects various downstream processes, including DNA methylation and neurotransmitter synthesis, ultimately contributing to intellectual disability and abnormal facial shape. Similarly, loss-of-function mutations in HNMT disrupt the methylation of histamine, potentially impacting downstream signaling pathways that also converge on methionine metabolism or SAM availability, leading to shared phenotypes.

**How to falsify it:** The discovery of loss-of-function variants in AHCY or HNMT that are present at a frequency greater than 1% in the gnomAD database would falsify the causal link for these specific variants. _(variant: gnomAD allele frequency > 0.01)_

**Why it matters:** Targeting the SAH/SAM cycle or related metabolic pathways could offer therapeutic avenues for both AHCY-related disease and intellectual disability, autosomal recessive 51, by restoring metabolic balance and downstream molecular functions.
